Sinai Covenant
SY-ny-eye KUV-uh-nunt
noun phrase (biblical-theological concept)
From Hebrew Sinai (the mountain of God in the wilderness of Sin, exact etymology disputed — possibly from seneh, thornbush, from the burning bush theophany of Exod 3, or from the ancient deity Sin, a moon-god associated with the region) + Hebrew berit (covenant, agreement, bond, from a root possibly related to bara, to cut, since ancient covenants were ratified by cutting animals — Gen 15; Jer 34:18). The Sinai covenant (also called the Mosaic covenant, the covenant of the law, or the old covenant) is the bilateral covenant God made with Israel at Mount Sinai (Horeb), mediated through Moses, ratified by blood, and documented in the Mosaic law.

Biblical Definition

The Sinai covenant is God's covenant with the nation of Israel, made at Mount Sinai (Horeb) in the wilderness following the Exodus from Egypt, mediated through Moses, ratified by the blood of oxen sprinkled on the altar and on the people (Exod 24:6–8), and documented in the book of the Law (Exod 20–23; Deuteronomy). The covenant was proposed by God (Exod 19:3–6) and accepted by Israel's acclamation: “And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient.” (Exod 24:7). It was structured as a suzerainty treaty (similar to ancient Near Eastern treaties between a great king and a vassal nation), with God as the sovereign and Israel as the covenant people: prologue (Exod 20:1–2), stipulations (the Decalogue and case law), ratification ceremony, and sanctions (blessings and curses in Deut 27–28). The Sinai covenant was administrated in the Mosaic law through the Levitical priesthood, the tabernacle/temple, the sacrificial system, and the Sabbath and feast calendar. Reformed covenant theology distinguishes the Sinai covenant as an administration of the covenant of grace (not a separate covenant of works for national blessing) while acknowledging its unique national and typological features. The New Testament treats the Sinai covenant as the “old covenant” (2 Cor 3:14; Heb 8:6–13), which has been fulfilled, superseded, and replaced by the new covenant in Christ's blood (Luke 22:20; Heb 8:13). The Mosaic law's moral content (the Ten Commandments) is not abolished but reaffirmed under the new covenant; its ceremonial content (priesthood, sacrifices, calendar) has been fulfilled in Christ and discontinued; its civil/national content applied to the theocratic state of Israel and does not bind the church.

Webster 1828 Definition

The covenant God made with Israel at Mount Sinai through Moses — ratified by blood, documented in the Mosaic law, administered through Levitical priesthood and tabernacle worship; the “old covenant” that Reformed theology identifies as an administration of the covenant of grace, now fulfilled and superseded by the new covenant in Christ's blood.

SINAI COVENANT, n. The covenant of the LORD with Israel at Mount Sinai (Horeb), mediated by Moses (Exod 19–24), ratified by the sprinkling of blood (Exod 24:6–8), documented in the book of the Law, and administered through Levitical priesthood, tabernacle worship, and the Mosaic law-code.

2. STRUCTURE (suzerainty-treaty form): historical prologue (“I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of Egypt”, Exod 20:1–2) → stipulations (Decalogue + case law) → covenant document (the book of the covenant) → blessings and curses (Deut 27–28) → succession arrangements.

3. REFORMED TAXONOMY: the Sinai covenant is an administration of the one covenant of grace (not a covenant of works inserted between Abraham and Christ) that served the typological and pedagogical function of preserving Israel, pointing to Christ through its sacrificial system and Levitical types, and serving as a “schoolmaster” to bring Israel to Christ (Gal 3:24).

4. OLD COVENANT STATUS: 2 Corinthians 3:14; Hebrews 8:6–13 — the Sinai covenant is the “old covenant,” now obsolete and vanishing, because Christ is its fulfillment and the new covenant in his blood renders its ceremonial apparatus fulfilled and therefore discontinued.

5. MORAL LAW CONTINUITY: the Decalogue embedded in the Sinai covenant retains its moral binding force under the new covenant (the “third use of the law”) because it expresses the unchanging moral character of God — only the ceremonial and civil law-categories peculiar to Israel's theocracy have been discontinued.

Key Scripture

Exod 24:7 — "And he took the book of the covenant, and read in the audience of the people: and they said, All that the LORD hath said will we do, and be obedient."

Exod 24:8 — "And Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, Behold the blood of the covenant, which the LORD hath made with you concerning all these words."

Deut 5:2 — "The LORD our God made a covenant with us in Horeb."

Heb 8:6 — "But now hath he obtained a more excellent ministry, by how much also he is the mediator of a better covenant, which was established upon better promises."

Modern Corruption

Two errors corrupt the Sinai covenant's role in biblical theology: hyper-dispensationalism, which treats the Sinai covenant as a separate works-covenant entirely distinct from the covenant of grace; and antinomianism, which treats the Sinai covenant's fulfillment in Christ as the abolition of the moral law's binding force.

expand to see more

Classic dispensationalism (Scofield, Chafer) treats the Sinai covenant as a conditional works-covenant inserted between the Abrahamic and new covenants — an offer of the kingdom to Israel that was forfeited by Israel's rejection of Jesus, now postponed to the millennium. This reading creates a fundamental discontinuity within the one covenant of grace that Reformed covenant theology insists Scripture forbids: Galatians 3:17 explicitly says the Mosaic law 430 years after Abraham “does not invalidate a covenant previously ratified by God.” The Sinai covenant was not a competing covenant of merit; it was an administration of the same Abrahamic promise, with typological and pedagogical features appropriate to Israel's national phase of redemptive history.

The antinomian error moves in the opposite direction: if the “old covenant” is obsolete (Heb 8:13), then the law it carried — including the moral law — is no longer binding on Christians. But Paul's treatment of the Decalogue in the new covenant context (Rom 7:7–12; 13:8–10; Eph 6:1–3; 1 Cor 7:19) assumes the moral law's continued validity; only the Mosaic ceremonial law has been fulfilled and discontinued. The 1689 Confession (19.1–5) carefully distinguishes the moral, ceremonial, and judicial law of Sinai, maintaining the full binding force of the moral law while affirming the ceremonial law's fulfillment in Christ.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Sinai covenant's structural template is the ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaty (Lord-vassal treaty), which God adapted to reveal the covenantal character of his relationship with Israel — patterned on, and fulfilling, the earlier Abrahamic covenant.

expand to see more

Hebrew berit — covenant, from a root related to cutting (karat berit = to cut a covenant); ratification by blood-cutting (Exod 24:6–8) follows the ancient pattern of Gen 15 and Jer 34:18

Ancient Near Eastern suzerainty treaty: the Hittite treaty pattern (historical prologue, stipulations, sanctions, deposition, witnesses, succession) underlies the Sinai covenant's structure — God adapted a culturally recognizable political form to reveal his covenant relationship

Hebrew Sinai — the mountain of God, site of theophany (the burning bush, Exod 3; the cloud and thunder, Exod 19; the giving of the law, Exod 20) and covenant ratification (Exod 24)

Paul's allegory (Gal 4:24–25): Sinai = the covenant of bondage (Hagar) vs. Jerusalem above = the covenant of freedom (Sarah) — Paul uses Sinai typologically for legalistic law-keeping divorced from grace, not for the Sinai covenant as a whole

Westminster Confession 19.1–5: distinguishes the moral law (universal, perpetual, Decalogue-expressed), the ceremonial law (typological, fulfilled in Christ, abrogated), and the judicial law (Israel's national polity, expired with the theocracy) within the Mosaic administration

Usage

"Hebrews 8–10 presents Christ as the fulfillment and replacement of every major element of the Sinai covenant: he is the better high priest (7:26–28), the mediator of a better covenant (8:6), the offeror of a better sacrifice (9:13–14), and the guarantor of better promises (8:6) — not abrogating the pattern but fulfilling it so completely that the copy is retired."

"The Mosaic covenant's blood-ratification (Exod 24:8) is explicitly cited by Jesus at the Last Supper (“This cup is the new covenant in my blood,” Luke 22:20) — the Sinai covenant's blood becomes the interpretive key for the cross, and the cross fulfills and supersedes what the Sinai blood only typologically pointed to."

"Martin Luther's theology of law and gospel distinguishes the covenant law's condemning function (driving sinners to Christ) from its directing function (guiding the regenerate in righteousness), both of which Luther rooted in the Mosaic-Sinai framework operating within the one covenant of grace."
